formulas.text: Total = average × count     Average = total ÷ count
formulas.note: Convert every average to a total before doing anything else.

formulas.text: Missing part = total − (sum of the known parts)
formulas.note: Numbers that are given but not needed (a distractor) are common.
A ratio 3 : 4 : 6 can be used as the n's directly.

formulas.text: Average of evenly spaced numbers = (first + last) ÷ 2
formulas.note: First multiple above the lower limit, last multiple below the upper limit.

q-av-parts.cue: An average of some numbers, averages of some of them, and a number or a sub-group's average is asked.
q-av-parts.standard: Total = average × count for the whole set and for each known part. Subtract the known parts from the whole, then divide by how many numbers are left.
q-av-parts.fast: Work with the differences from the overall average: each part's surplus or deficit must cancel. 13 numbers at 75: the six at 69 are 6×(−6) = −36 and the six at 80 are 6×5 = +30, so the 7th is 75 + 6 = 81.
q-av-parts.eliminate: The missing value must lie on the other side of the overall average from the part that is short. If the known groups average below the overall average, the leftover is above it.
traps: Using the wrong count when dividing (11th and 12th are two numbers, not one).
Using a clue that is not needed, such as '11th is 12 more than the 12th', when only the sum of the two matters.

q-av-weighted.cue: Several groups with their own averages and sizes (or a ratio of sizes), and the overall average is asked.
q-av-weighted.standard: Multiply each group's average by its weight, add, divide by the total weight.
q-av-weighted.fast: Start from the lowest average and add the surplus: 17 + (0×3 + 2×4 + 6×6) ÷ 13 = 17 + 44/13 = 20.38.
q-av-weighted.eliminate: The overall average is pulled towards the biggest group, here 23 (weight 6), so it is above the simple mean 19.67. Strike options below it.
traps: Taking the simple mean of the group averages.
Dividing by the number of groups instead of the total weight.

q-av-spaced.cue: 'Average of all integers between a and b that are divisible by k.'
q-av-spaced.standard: List the first and last multiples inside the range, then the average is their mean.
q-av-spaced.fast: First multiple = k × (smallest whole number above a/k); last = k × (largest below b/k). 150 ÷ 13 ≈ 11.5 → 13×12 = 156; 300 ÷ 13 ≈ 23.07 → 13×23 = 299. (156 + 299) ÷ 2 = 227.5.
q-av-spaced.eliminate: The answer is the middle of the two end multiples, so it sits near the middle of the range and is a multiple of 0.5 (k × (m + n) ÷ 2).
traps: Using the limits themselves (150 and 300) instead of the first and last multiples.
Including a limit that is not a multiple.

pyqs.text: What is the average of all integers between 150 and 300 that are exactly divisible by 13?
solution: Multiples of 13 in range: 13×12 = 156 up to 13×23 = 299.
They are evenly spaced, so the average is (156 + 299) ÷ 2 = 227.5.
pyqs.trick: Find only the two end multiples (156 and 299) and halve their sum.

pyqs.text: The average of 12 numbers is 75. The average of the first 5 is 68. The average of the next 5 is 20% more than the average of the first 5. The 11th number is 12 more than the 12th. Find the average of the 11th and 12th numbers.
solution: Total of 12 numbers = 12 × 75 = 900. First five total = 5 × 68 = 340.
Last two total = 900 − 340 − 408 = 152, so their average = 76. (The '12 more' clue is not needed.)
pyqs.trick: The 11th and 12th together are all that is left, so only their sum matters; ignore the '12 more' clue.

pyqs.text: In a group of 60 workers the average monthly income is ₹28,000. If 20 junior workers average ₹18,000 each, find the average income of the senior workers.
pyqs.trick: Juniors are 10,000 below 28,000 and there are 20 of them; the 40 seniors must make it up: 20 × 10,000 ÷ 40 = 5,000 above, so 33,000.

pyqs.text: What is the average of all integers between 200 and 350 that are exactly divisible by 11?
solution: First multiple above 200 is 11 × 19 = 209. Last below 350 is 11 × 31 = 341.
pyqs.trick: The answer is the midpoint of 209 and 341, and the midpoint of two multiples of 11 with an odd count is a multiple of 11 itself. Only 275 and 286 are, and 286 is too high.

c.note: Does not match the worked answer, which is option (a) 275.

b.note: The average of evenly spaced multiples of 11 with an odd count of terms is itself a multiple of 11, and 272 is not.

d.note: Same test: 292 is not a multiple of 11.
